subject: ecce
title: Model Question Paper 3
meta: Time: 3 hours · Maximum marks: 80 · Modelled on the April 2026 NIOS paper
instructions: All questions are compulsory. Where a question has OR, answer either one.
Section A: 16 MCQs (1 mark each); a reading passage with six 1-mark questions; nine questions with two parts of 1 mark each (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks, one-word answers).
Section B: 2-mark answers in 30–50 words, 3-mark answers in 50–80 words, 5-mark answers in 80–120 words.
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: What does the home and school language divide indicate?
questions.answer: A situation where the medium of instruction at school is different from the language used at home.

questions.q: According to NCF 2005, how should India's linguistic diversity be seen?
questions.answer: As a resource to promote multilingual proficiency in a child.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Indian Constitution aims to protect the ________ nature of India.
Which languages should be valued equally?
questions.answer: All languages, including tribal languages as well as English.

questions.q: How does NCF 2005 propose to handle first-generation learners?
questions.answer: Teach them in the mother tongue in the initial years, with less stress on a second and third language.

questions.q: Why is less stress put on a second and third language for first-generation learners?
questions.answer: Because support to learn these languages may not be available to the child at home.

sections.passage: India is a multilingual country, and its Constitution is committed to protecting the multilingual nature of India. The home and school language divide indicates the situation where the medium of instruction at school is different from the language used at home. NCF, 2005 respects the multilingual character of Indian society and suggests it should be seen as a resource to promote multilingual proficiency in a child. All languages, including tribal languages as well as English, should be valued equally. All mother tongues are appreciated as an important link between the young child and the school. In the case of a first-generation learner, teaching in the initial years should be in the mother tongue, with less stress on learning a second and third language, as support may not be available to the child at home to learn these languages. (October 2024)

Answer in one sentence: As an ECCE teacher, mention one intervention you would take for a child having difficulty in reading and writing.
questions.answer: For example: give extra sound- and visual-discrimination games, rhymes and letter-sound matching in small steps with picture cards, observe the child systematically, share the concern with parents and refer the child to a special educator for assessment.
questions.note: The real question had three 1-mark parts; this part is from April 2026. Lesson 22.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why are the first six years of life considered crucial for development?
questions.answer: They are a time of very fast growth and development in all domains, and 90% of brain development takes place by six. Any deprivation then (poor nutrition, health care or stimulation) can cause developmental delays, while quality care and early learning lay the base for later learning.
questions.note: October 2024 asked this as an MCQ ('time for rapid development'). Lesson 1.

questions.q: What do you mean by a curriculum framework? Comment on the National Curriculum Framework (NCF), 2005.
questions.answer: A curriculum framework is a comprehensive, organised set of guidelines on what and how children at a stage should learn, including assessment, to reach the desired outcomes. NCF 2005, prepared by NCERT, asks that young children get care and experiences for holistic development and recommends a play-based, developmentally appropriate ECCE as preparation for school.

questions.q: What is symbolic function?
questions.answer: The preschooler's ability to keep an image of an object, person or event in mind and think about it without it being present, and to name it with symbols such as words and numbers.
questions.note: October 2022 asked for a one-sentence explanation. Lesson 9.

questions.q: List some ways of noting children's progress in an ECCE centre.
questions.answer: Regular observation of each child in all domains, daily records and diary notes, checklists of milestones, portfolios of children's work, and comparing with age norms; sharing these with parents.

questions.q: Differentiate between pre-primary readiness and school readiness.
questions.answer: Pre-primary readiness prepares a child for a preschool, which is less structured, like an extension of day care: basic knowledge, social skills, independence in self-help, communication and health. School readiness prepares a child for formal schooling with more complex activities for reading, writing and number work: following rules and routines, working alone, focusing and listening, and language, maths and general knowledge.

or.q: Describe any two factors important to successful transition in children.
or.answer: Any two: building on children's prior and current practices; giving children an active role in preparing for transitions with their families; helping them understand the routines and practices of the new setting; helping them negotiate changes in status or identity; and working collaboratively among parents, teachers and schools.

questions.q: Why is early identification of disabilities in children important? How can a teacher identify children with difficulty in reading and writing?
questions.answer: Early identification allows help while the young brain is most able to change, and greatly reduces later social, behavioural and learning difficulties. Signs of reading and writing difficulty: slow naming of objects and colours, weak rhyming and syllable blending, little interest in print, trouble learning letters and letter-sound connections.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: How do families need to accommodate children with special conditions, and what challenges do they face?
questions.answer: Children with disabilities are among the most excluded; many do not complete primary education. Families must meet their special requirements, which often need extra care, time, money and therapy from parents, and help them join mainstream schools. Siblings and other children need counselling to understand differences and reach out with empathy.

or.q: What are the challenges faced by migrant children, particularly those of families employed in the unorganised sector?
or.answer: An estimated 4–6 million children are affected by migration. Their families face exclusion from basic services, exploitative work (no minimum wages, no social security), gender-based wage discrimination and denial of maternity rights and childcare. Seasonal migration disrupts schooling and often denies the child's right to education.

questions.q: Describe the development of language in children.
questions.answer: Infants communicate by crying, laughing and cooing; around four months they play with sounds; from 6–7 months cooing becomes babbling ('baba', 'mama'); they also use gestures. These are pre-speech forms. Speech forms follow: comprehension develops before speech, pronunciation becomes clear, vocabulary grows rapidly, and children move from two- or three-word phrases ('give me food') to sentences and complex sentences. In middle childhood they learn the social rules of using language with different people.

questions.q: What are the two important functions of the placenta? Mention the stage of prenatal development in which it forms.
questions.answer: Functions: (1) it passes oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood to the embryo or foetus, nourishing it; (2) it removes waste materials from the embryo or foetus. The placenta forms in the germinal stage (the first two weeks after conception).

or.q: Describe any three reflexes in a newborn.
or.answer: Rooting: the infant turns the head towards anything that touches the cheek. Palmar grasp: closes the fingers and grasps an object placed in the palm. Moro: when support for the head and neck is suddenly removed, thrusts the arms out and seems to grasp. (Others: Babinski — toes fan out when the outer sole is stroked; startle; eye blink; sucking; stepping.)

questions.q: Explain the significance of sensory stimulation for development.
questions.answer: Infants learn about the world through their senses. Stimulation through sight, sound, smell, taste and touch creates neural pathways in the brain that support later learning, and develops motor skills and the ability to solve simple problems. Visual stimulation (faces, colours, peek-a-boo) builds observation; auditory input (talking, music, natural sounds) builds the base of language; touch (holding, rocking, textures) builds trust and fine motor skills; movement builds balance. Activities should be many and repeated.
questions.note: October 2022 also asked about kinaesthetic stimulation. Lesson 10.

questions.q: Explain the importance of accounting and social auditing.
questions.answer: Social accounting and auditing record and report the social and environmental effects of an organisation's economic actions to interest groups and society. It checks performance against social, environmental and economic objectives and values. Objectives: effective use of resources; an ongoing record of how the centre has changed; feedback on how things are going; knowing what works well and what does not; knowing how far aims are achieved; and collecting information for grant applications and reports.

questions.q: What steps will you take to ensure gender-equitable participation of children in a preschool?
questions.answer: Choose toys and materials for the skills they develop, not by the child's sex, and prefer gender-neutral toys such as puzzles, blocks and clay; choose stories carefully and discuss role reversals; encourage fair play — all toys within reach of all and structured time for every child with the kitchen set, ball and swings, outdoor games for all; encourage friendships and mixed teams; avoid gender-based work distribution and invite both boys and girls to help with food or tidying.

or.q: What are the implications of multilingualism for an ECCE centre?
or.answer: Children of different home languages study together; if instruction is only in another language they struggle, lose confidence and may drop out. So the centre should respect and use the home language, build the second and third language on its strengths, use local stories, songs and riddles, value sign language and Braille, and see multilingualism as a resource (NCF 2005).

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the term 'play'. Suggest the steps you would take to identify equipment and materials for outdoor play for children of 4–6 years.
questions.answer: Play is a child's freely chosen, joyful, creative activity of mind and body without externally imposed goals; Montessori called it the work of the child. Steps: (1) observe the children's interests, abilities and needs, including those with disabilities; (2) list equipment for large-muscle activities — running, climbing, jumping, sliding, swinging, balancing: balance beams, slides, swings, merry-go-round, jungle gym, materials for group games (ball, bat), water play, sand pit, tricycles; (3) check safety, sturdiness, size and height, and enough pieces for the group; (4) plan the space — paths for tricycles, sand and water areas, fixed swings and slides, open green space — so supervision is easy; (5) prefer low-cost and local materials such as old tyres; (6) rearrange with the seasons and review use.

or.q: Describe play activities in the context of children. Discuss the role of the teacher in promoting children's play in a centre.
or.answer: Play activities cover all domains: cognitive and language (puzzles, sorting, stories, role play), affective (dramatisation, songs, dressing dolls), psychomotor (throwing, jumping, threading beads, clay). Teacher's role: observer — watches how children interact and use materials, to plan better play; facilitator — arranges equipment and climate, lets children speak freely and encourages questions; reviewer — checks after each activity whether it met each child's needs and the curriculum goals, and informs parents; organiser — prepares a safe, happy, interesting and challenging indoor and outdoor play environment with suitable materials.

questions.q: What are the roles and responsibilities of ECCE teachers in planning activities and creating an enriching teaching-learning environment?
questions.answer: Planning: the teacher plans the curriculum, timetable, age-appropriate indoor and outdoor activities, assessment procedures, parent-teacher meetings and workshops, keeping in mind children's needs, society's expectations and the resources available; planning must be thoughtful and systematic. She also helps design and implement the curriculum. Enriching environment: organise and manage the classroom — allocate space for different activities, select age-appropriate equipment and materials, arrange space for children with disabilities and ensure safety; use a variety of teaching-learning materials, including locally available low-cost and no-cost materials and recycled objects, used in many ways (pebbles for counting and textures); organise developmentally appropriate experiences such as role play and park visits; ensure that every child feels respected, accepted and welcomed; and assess regularly through observation, anecdotal records and portfolios.
